newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Mother Teresa order rescues children in Albania.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa order rescues children in Albania.

text.p: Nuns working for Mother Teresa's missionary order in Albania staged a dramatic rescue of the mentally handicapped children they care for after rampaging gunmen burned out nearby buildings.

A bank and other houses next door to the compound of the Missionaries of Charity order in the town of Shkoder were reduced to blackened shells during two days of mayhem last week, when thousands of guns were looted from army barracks.

The order's Mother Superior in Shkoder, Maria Goreti, told Reuters on Tuesday that she feared her own building where the sisters care for 25 mentally handicapped children would be engulfed in the flames.
"Fire was coming into the compound, the houses nearby were burning," she said.
"We called the priests from the Jesuit seminary and they rescued us in their cars. The children were crying and screaming, they were so disturbed that they never slept that night," Goreti said.
Shkoder, the regional capital of northern Albania, has in recent days started to pull itself back from the brink of anarchy that has gripped the country in recent weeks.

Unrest started in the south of the country after the collapse of shady pyramid investment schemes which bankrupted thousands of families. Angry citizens looted weapons and seized control of towns as the mayhem spread throughout the country.
Goreti and the other 13 sisters in Shkoder have now been able to bring the children back to the compound, but they still employ two armed guards to protect them at night.
Local authorities are still trying to persuade people to hand in their looted weapons, but concede it will be a difficult task.
"Almost every family here in the city has a gun," said Elham Sharra, the local prefect.

The sisters also believe in the power of prayer in a city where at least nine people have been killed in an orgy of random shooting and roadblocks erected at the height of the violence still clutter the streets, although they are no longer manned.
"Prayer will keep the devil away," said Goreti, a tiny bird-like figure dressed in a blue-edged white habit and headscarf who looks remarkably like a younger version of her order's founder.
"Our sisters are praying for us and our Mother Teresa is praying for us."
Mother Teresa, born Agnes Goinxha Bejaxhiu in Skopje in 1910, has become the world's most famous Albanian for her missionary work in Calcutta.
She established her order in Albania in 1991 after the collapse of an isolationist Communist regime that had turned the country into an officially atheist state for 23 years.
There are seven contemplative brothers of the same order in the nearby town of Bushat. They came to help the sisters in Shkoder as soon as they heard of their plight.
The brothers were taken aback by the suddenness of the violence, and feared it might have tipped Albania into the abyss.
Brother Simon, a 39-year-old Briton, said the violence had been worsened by the fact that jails were emptied during the recent chaos.
Brother Simon, whose family live in East Peckham, southeast England, said he had joined the order after giving up a career as an officer in the British army.
"I'm now a soldier of Christ, which is much better," he said.
